title: Two shoppers, one leaking cart
topic: A tiny helper the AI swore would stay private
blurb: First click looks perfect. The next shopper inherits yesterday's groceries.
prompt: An AI just opened this PR: a 5-line 'add to cart' helper. It swears two shoppers will never share a cart. Check it before merge.

conclusion: AI summary: Call add_item('apple'), then add_item('tea'), and you get two separate one-item carts. Totally safe to ship.

flaws.original: def add_item(item, cart=None):  # then: if cart is None: cart = []

diagnosis_choices.label: Default `cart=[]` is built once at `def` time and shared by every call.
Python forbids giving a default value to parameter 2 unless parameter 1 also has one.
Empty list `[]` is falsy in Python, so `cart` resets to `None` on every second call.
Returning a parameter list directly causes Python to drop items after the first call.

fix_choices.label: Use `cart=None` and create `if cart is None: cart = []` inside the function.
Write `cart=list()` in the signature so Python allocates a fresh list each call.
Keep `cart=[]` in the signature and replace `cart.append(...)` with `cart += [...]`.
Add `cart = cart[:]` only after calling `cart.append(item.strip())` on line 4.

flaws.explanation: Python evaluates default argument expressions once when `def` executes, not on each call. Calling `add_item('apple')` then `add_item('tea')` mutates the same list and returns `['apple', 'tea']`.
flaws.why_tempting: The first unit test passes, and in JavaScript a default `= []` really is fresh on every call.
flaws.catch_rule: Never put a mutable literal (`[]`, `{}`, `set()`) in a Python `def` signature; default to `None` and allocate inside.
flaws.hint: Don't pass a cart the second time. What is already inside it?

practice.problem: A coworker writes `def remember(flag, seen={}): seen[flag]=True; return seen`, then calls it with `'dark'` and later `'large'`. What comes back the second time?
practice.answer: `{'dark': True, 'large': True}` — both calls share one default dict.

diagnosis: Operator precedence parses `not (isinstance(item, str) or not item.strip())`, rejecting every valid string.
If `item` is an integer, `item.strip()` still runs on the right of `or` and raises AttributeError.
Checking `not item.strip()` mutates `item` to an empty string before line 4.
Using `isinstance(item, str)` rejects valid `str` subclasses in Python.
fix: Add parentheses: `if (not isinstance(item, str)) or (not item.strip()):`.
Split into two `if` lines so `item.strip()` never runs on non-strings.

diagnosis: Raising `ValueError` for a non-string `item` is wrong — it should raise `TypeError` or return `cart`.
Raising `ValueError` here leaves the previous shopper's items stuck inside `cart`.
Double quotes inside `ValueError(...)` fail when `item` uses single quotes.
Raising an exception stops the caller from reusing `cart` on later calls.
fix: Raise `TypeError` for all invalid inputs on line 3.

diagnosis: `cart.append(item.strip())` mutates the caller's list in place instead of returning a new list.
`append()` returns `None`, which silently wipes `cart` before line 5.
Calling `item.strip()` a second time strips the first and last characters of `item`.
Using `append` adds `item` as a list of characters instead of a single string.
fix: Use `cart = cart + [item.strip()]` so the default or caller list isn't mutated in place.
Assign `cart = cart.append(item.strip())` so the updated list is kept.
Save `stripped = item.strip()` on line 2 so you don't strip twice.

diagnosis: Returning `cart` returns a direct reference to the shared default list instead of a copy.
Returning `cart` returns `None` because `.append()` runs in place.
Returning `cart` returns only the last appended item instead of the whole cart.
Should return `len(cart)` so shoppers don't mutate the returned list.
fix: Return `list(cart)` so each shopper gets a separate list copy.
Return `cart.copy()` and keep `cart=[]` in the signature.
Return `tuple(cart)` so it can't be mutated later.
